ai-at-work.title: Crusoe raises $3.9B to build massive data centers and small modular ‘AI factories’
ai-at-work.excerpt: The round values the data center giant at $30.9 billion.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Crusoe Energy just closed a 3.9 billion dollar funding round that values the company at nearly 31 billion dollars, positioning them to build massive data centers and smaller modular AI processing facilities. This matters to digital workplace teams because the infrastructure race is heating up, which means compute availability, latency, and costs for AI tools your organization actually uses will shift in the coming years. Look, another well-funded data center play isn't exactly breaking news, but the "modular AI factory" angle suggests someone finally figured out that not every organization needs a Vegas-sized server farm to run their copilot.

ai-at-work.title: The FAA’s plan to fix air traffic? $875M worth of AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: A new AI-based software program is being launched to help air traffic controllers better navigate their jobs as the crossing guards of America's skies.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The FAA is investing $875 million in AI software to help air traffic controllers manage their workload more effectively. For digital workplace pros, this is a textbook example of how enterprise software adoption at scale demands serious change management beyond just throwing money at the problem. Here's the thing though: air traffic controllers have been doing this job for decades with existing tools, so the real question isn't whether the AI works, it's whether anyone actually uses it when lives depend on the radio call they're about to make.

ai-at-work.title: Microsoft exec called AI scraping ‘the largest theft of labor in human history,’ new unredacted filings reveal
ai-at-work.excerpt: Newly unsealed court filings show Microsoft privately called OpenAI's data practices "theft" while both companies scraped paywalled Times content, built datasets from it, and warned internally it woul
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A Microsoft executive privately called AI training data scraping "the largest theft of labor in human history," according to unredacted court documents, even while Microsoft itself was doing the exact same scraping alongside OpenAI. This matters to digital workplace pros because your organization's content, customer data, and employee knowledge are being hoovered up by these companies to train AI tools you're probably already buying and deploying. The irony is so thick you could spread it on toast: Microsoft calling theft "theft" while standing knee-deep in the same stolen goods is either peak hypocrisy or the most honest accidental confession Silicon Valley has given us in years.

ai-at-work.title: Full speed ahead: Despite calls to slow AI down, its support structure is on the fast track
ai-at-work.excerpt: While tech titans at Salesforce Inc.’s Dreamforce event in San Francisco this week engaged in a spirited debate over whether the pace of deployment for artificial intelligence should be slowed, a grou
ai-at-work.dwp_take: While some tech leaders debate whether AI deployment should pump the brakes, others are simultaneously building out the infrastructure to accelerate it further. Digital workplace pros need to pay attention because this infrastructure buildout will determine what AI capabilities actually land in their tech stacks, regardless of what the talking heads say about responsible deployment. It's like watching someone argue about speed limits while their buddy is already pouring concrete for a ten lane highway.

tools-tech.title: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait
tools-tech.excerpt: Claude Code Projects could change how developers manage complex AI coding workflows by coordinating threads, sharing memory, and spanning repos, but its biggest benefits are still cloud-only for now.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic rolled out upgrades to Claude Code Projects that let developers orchestrate multiple AI threads, share context across workstreams, and jump between repositories, though these fancy features only work in the cloud right now. Local developers who want this stuff running on their own machines are basically stuck watching from the sidelines, which matters because plenty of teams still can't or won't push sensitive code to the cloud. It's the classic tech move: dangle the shiny new toy, then make sure it only works in someone else's backyard.

tools-tech.title: An undisclosed Microsoft presentation is now central to a multi-million dollar antitrust fight
tools-tech.excerpt: There’s a new development in a Microsoft antitrust case, originally filed in England’s High Court in April 2021, and it doesn’t look good for the tech giant. A consent order from the UK Competition Ap
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is being forced by UK courts to hand over internal presentations to ValueLicens, a reseller claiming the company unfairly blocked them from the secondhand software market. This matters because it shows how platform gatekeeping decisions get scrutinized legally, and those decisions are often made in meetings that leave digital trails. Here's the thing: after 30 years watching tech companies, I can tell you that the documents they fight hardest to keep hidden are always the ones worth reading.

tools-tech.title: Anthropic tries to make Claude stickier with launch of Docs and Slides
tools-tech.excerpt: Anthropic is equipping its Claude AI assistant for more productivity work with the launch of Claude Docs and Slides. While it’s already possible to create documents such as Microsoft Word and Google D
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic launched Claude Docs and Slides, native document and presentation tools built directly into Claude's interface, making it easier for users to create and edit content without switching applications. This matters because digital workplace teams are increasingly evaluating AI tools as core productivity platforms rather than point solutions, and feature parity with Microsoft and Google is now table stakes in that competition. The irony is that every AI vendor is now rushing to build the same basic Office suite, which means we're probably going to spend the next three years comparing whose spelling checker is least annoying.

tools-tech.title: Will Apple enter the server business?
tools-tech.excerpt: In a world of speculation, this week’s most interesting rumor says Apple may plan to enter the server business once again, with powerful systems running its own Apple Silicon chips. It’s hard to dismi
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple is apparently considering re-entering the traditional server market with custom Apple Silicon chips, though they're technically already building servers for their Private Cloud Compute system. This matters because if Apple actually ships commercial servers, it could disrupt enterprise infrastructure decisions and force IT teams to evaluate yet another vendor in an already complicated ecosystem. Honestly, after thirty years watching Apple, I'd believe it when I see it actually shipping to paying customers, not when some analyst spots a supply chain rumor.

digital-culture.title: How to figure out which advice is worth taking
digital-culture.excerpt: If you are ambitious in your goals for work and want to continue improving your performance, then you’re going to get a lot of advice from people. If you try to follow all the advice you get, you’ll b
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece about filtering advice rather than blindly chasing every suggestion that comes your way. This matters to digital workplace folks because we live in an advice hellscape where everyone from LinkedIn influencers to your cousin's friend has a hot take on how you should work, communicate, and organize your team. The real skill isn't collecting wisdom like Pokemon cards—it's knowing which advice actually applies to your situation and which is just noise from someone selling a course.

digital-culture.title: Warren Buffett, Richard Branson, and Satya Nadella feel their hobbies make them more successful. Science says they’re right
digital-culture.excerpt: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says playing cricket taught him lessons about teamwork and leadership—put your team first, and bring out the best in other people—that have stayed with him throughout his c
digital-culture.dwp_take: Three tech billionaires credit hobbies with boosting their leadership and productivity, and research backs up the connection between outside interests and professional success. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it validates what we've known for years: forcing people to optimize every waking hour kills creativity and actually tanks performance. The irony is thick here, since these guys made billions while advocating for something most corporate cultures actively punish with back-to-back meetings and Slack notifications on weekends.

digital-culture.title: How to keep your job in the AI age without knowing AI
digital-culture.excerpt: Artificial intelligence is reshaping every industry, but staying relevant doesn’t require learning to code or becoming a data scientist. This guide draws on insights from career strategists and organi
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is arguing that technical AI skills aren't essential for job security, and that soft skills like adaptability and judgment will protect workers from automation. This matters because most digital workplace professionals manage people and processes, not algorithms, so understanding how to lead through change beats memorizing Python syntax. Honestly, this is the workplace equivalent of telling someone not to panic during an earthquake, which is fine advice until the building actually collapses around them.

digital-culture.title: ‘Bah, humbug!’ Could employee apathy mean curtains for the traditional holiday party?
digital-culture.excerpt: People say they prefer cash or time off, though some argue office gatherings are still beneficial
digital-culture.dwp_take: Employees are increasingly skipping company holiday parties and saying they'd rather have cash bonuses or extra time off instead. This matters because it forces workplace leaders to reconsider whether mandatory festive gatherings actually build culture or just drain budgets on eggnog nobody drinks. Here's the thing: if your holiday party requires a survey to prove people want to be there, you've already lost the room, so maybe just give them the money and let them celebrate with people they actually chose to spend time with.

industry-news.title: Siri AI Is Finally Here: 7 Things You Can Actually Do With It
industry-news.excerpt: Siri AI is rolling out with iOS 27. Here are seven things you can do with Apple’s upgraded assistant, plus supported iPhones and limitations. The post Siri AI Is Finally Here: 7 Things You Can Actuall
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple shipped an upgraded Siri with iOS 27 that finally does some useful things, though it comes with the usual limitations. Digital workplace pros need to pay attention because AI assistants are becoming workplace tools whether IT departments like it or not, and they'll need to figure out governance and security implications fast. Honestly, I've heard "Siri is finally useful" before, so I'll believe it when I see knowledge workers actually ditching their third-party tools for it.

industry-news.title: Google Cloud, Salesforce Tie Gemini Enterprise to Agentforce and CRM Data
industry-news.excerpt: Google Cloud and Salesforce are connecting Gemini Enterprise, Agentforce, Hyperforce, and Tableau to reduce integration friction for enterprise AI workflows. The post Google Cloud, Salesforce Tie Gemi
industry-news.dwp_take: Google and Salesforce just plugged their AI tools directly into each other so customers can run AI workflows without playing twenty questions with their tech stack. This matters because most digital workplaces are drowning in disconnected systems, and easier AI integration means your people might actually use these tools instead of letting them collect dust. Honestly, if this actually reduces integration friction as promised, it's one of the few moves that could make enterprise AI deployments less painful, though I'll believe it when I see it implemented at scale.

industry-news.title: Googlebook vs Chromebook: What’s Different About Google’s New Laptop?
industry-news.excerpt: Googlebook and Chromebook are both laptop families, but Google’s new flagship category adds deeper Android integration, new Gemini tools, and tighter phone connectivity. The post Googlebook vs Chromeb
industry-news.dwp_take: Google launched Googlebook as a new flagship laptop line with deeper Android integration, enhanced Gemini AI tools, and better phone connectivity compared to their existing Chromebook lineup. This matters because digital workplace teams need to understand whether this represents a real shift in device strategy or just marketing rebranding, which affects procurement decisions and end-user support plans. After thirty years in this space, I'm cautiously skeptical that tighter phone integration alone justifies another product category, but the AI tooling could actually be useful if Google resists the urge to cram every feature into every device.

industry-news.title: ViceForge Puts Four Video Editing Tools in One Browser Tab for Life
industry-news.excerpt: ViceForge Creator Elite combines AI clipping, manual editing, and live-stream capture in one browser tab. The post ViceForge Puts Four Video Editing Tools in One Browser Tab for Life appeared first on
industry-news.dwp_take: ViceForge Creator Elite bundled four separate video editing functions into a single browser-based tool with AI clipping, manual editing, and live-stream capture capabilities. For digital workplace teams drowning in SaaS subscriptions and app fatigue, consolidation tools like this matter because they reduce context switching and simplify workflows for remote and hybrid workers creating video content daily. Honestly, if this actually works without the usual "bundle bloat" where you get four mediocre tools instead of one good one, it could be a legitimate productivity win. We'll believe it when we see it in production environments though.
